sections.h2: Which county is your Tulsa house in?
sections.html:
Population here was 413,066 in the 2020 census, making Tulsa the second-largest city in Oklahoma, with a metro area of 1,034,123. The 201.85 square miles stretch across four counties: Tulsa, Osage, Rogers and Wagoner.

Your county picks the office that values the house and the office that mails the tax bill. Nearly all Tulsa houses are in Tulsa County, yet a parcel near the city limits may fall under Osage, Rogers or Wagoner County instead, and each has its own assessor and treasurer. Read the county name on your tax statement before you phone any office.

Schools split the same way. Seven districts (Tulsa, Berryhill, Bixby, Broken Arrow, Jenks, Owasso and Union) cover the Tulsa County side, while Tulsa Public Schools covers the Osage County side. Buyers ask which district applies, so find out first.

Tulsa is a set of very different areas, and where a house sits changes how it is priced and who shops for it.

  • Downtown: about 1.4 square miles inside the Inner Dispersal Loop, with the Oil Capital Historic District, Blue Dome, Tulsa Arts District and Greenwood. Nearby are Owen Park, The Pearl, The Heights and Kendall-Whittier.
  • Midtown: the historic residential core, with early 20th-century homes in styles from art deco to Greek Revival in Maple Ridge, Swan Lake, Cherry Street, Brookside and Lortondale.
  • South Tulsa: mostly built since the 1970s, with lower-density suburban housing and retail.
  • East of Highway 169: a diverse area with much of the city's manufacturing.
  • West Tulsa: west of the Arkansas River, with large parks, reserves and oil refineries.

A century-old Midtown house and a 1980s south Tulsa ranch get different inspection questions. The older house draws questions about wiring, plumbing and foundations. The newer one draws questions about roof age and heating and cooling.

Spring and early summer storms in Tulsa can bring big hail, strong winds and now and then a tornado. May is the wettest month at 5.9 inches. A hail-beaten roof is a routine problem for sellers here.

Flooding shaped local rules. In 1984 a stalled front dumped 15 inches of rain overnight, killing 14 people and wrecking 7,000 buildings. Tulsa responded with one of the nation's most extensive flood control systems, which FEMA recognized for floodplain management in the early 1990s and again in 2000.

A house beside a creek or inside a mapped flood area will prompt the buyer's lender to ask about flood insurance. Triple-digit heat averages 11 days a year, so the air conditioning also lands on the inspection list. Pull any storm photos, repair estimates and insurance claim records before you list, because buyers ask for them.

sections.h2: Tulsa code enforcement and open violations
sections.html:
Tulsa's Code Enforcement handles nuisance, zoning and property maintenance rules for occupied, commercial and vacant properties. The office looks into about 22,000 violations across more than 18,000 cases a year. Reports go to 311 or tulsa311.com.

Violation stepWhat happens
Priority 1Unsecured structures, vehicles on blocks, blocked sidewalks, raw sewage
Priority 3Tall grass, trash, junk and debris, handled in order received
NoticeOwner gets 10 days to comply
ExtensionsUp to two 10-day extensions at $64 each, not available for every violation
AbatementIf the city does the work, the owner pays the cost plus a $300 processing fee

The city's "Up to Code" brochure adds that grass over 12 inches, unsecured vacant structures and inoperable vehicles stored outdoors are violations. An owner must board up a vacant structure after a fire, and openings left by a break-in must be secured right away.

Code cases for any address can be searched back to 2018 on the city's self-service portal, and buyers use it too. Plan on them finding an open case. Closing it out before you list spares you a late surprise.

sections.h2: Tulsa County property tax and key dates
sections.html:
Two county offices touch your bill. The Assessor fixes your home's value as of January 1, and the Treasurer then collects what is owed. Dates from the Assessor worth writing down:

  • Through March 15: file for most exemptions, homestead included. A late filing usually waits for the following year.
  • First Monday in April: final day for an informal appeal when no increase notice came in the mail.
  • May 31: Board of Equalization wraps up, though it can run until June 30.
  • September 15 to October 1: no owner or address changes while the roll is built.
  • October and November: the Treasurer receives the roll and mails the bills.

Half of the tax is due before January 1. Anyone paying in two parts owes the second part before April 1. Since ownership changes freeze each fall, a seller who closes in that window should check that the bill lands with the right person. Title companies normally prorate the year's tax between the two sides.

sections.h2: Ways to sell a house in Tulsa
sections.html:
You have three realistic paths. With neighborhoods this different, a price set for your block beats any citywide figure.

  • Agent listing: widest buyer pool, but expect prep work, showings and an appraisal for any financed buyer.
  • By owner: saves the commission, and leaves pricing and contracts to you.
  • Cash offer: fits houses carrying repairs, open code cases, tenants, hail damage or an estate.

A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal, the back-and-forth over repairs and the weeks waiting on loan approval. The title company handles payoffs at closing, so a lien or an unpaid city charge comes out of your proceeds instead of stopping the deal.

sections.h2: Closing day and what a cash sale skips
sections.html:
You close at a title company. There you sign the deed, any mortgage or lien gets paid off from the sale money, and you receive what is left. The year's property tax is divided between you and the buyer at that same table, so bring the latest county statement. If a code case remains open on the address, ask the title officer how it will be treated.

Cash means no lender sign-off, so no low appraisal and no loan that can collapse. Owners with hail-damaged roofs, tenants or an estate often pick it for that reason.

sections.h2: Documents to gather before you decide
sections.html:
Three papers help before any buyer calls: the code case history for your address, the county tax statement, and any storm or insurance claim records. Offers on Tulsa houses tend to move on those.

Print each open case from the city's code portal. Then read the county name on the tax statement and see whether the bill is paid up. Finally, gather hail photos, roof estimates and claim letters. Armed with these, you can weigh a listing, a sale by owner and a cash offer using real figures.

faqs.q: Is Tulsa only in Tulsa County?
faqs.a: No. The city reaches into Tulsa, Osage, Rogers and Wagoner Counties. Your tax statement shows which county's assessor and treasurer serve your address.

faqs.q: How do I report or look up a code violation in Tulsa?
faqs.a: Call 311 or use tulsa311.com to report one. The city's self-service portal lets you search code cases by address, with results going back to 2018.

faqs.q: How long do I have to fix a Tulsa code violation?
faqs.a: The notice gives the owner 10 days to comply. You can buy up to two 10-day extensions at $64 each, though some violations, such as unsecured structures, are not eligible.

faqs.q: When must I file for the homestead exemption in Tulsa County?
faqs.a: The Tulsa County Assessor accepts applications all year, but to count for the current year the application must be filed by March 15 or within 30 days of a valuation-increase notice.

faqs.q: Does hail damage stop me from selling a Tulsa house?
faqs.a: No. You can repair the roof and list the house, or sell it as is to a buyer who accounts for the damage. Keep photos, estimates and any insurance paperwork handy.
